I honestly almost started a blog at destructoid to write this, but decided I was less interested in my opinion than others. From where I am sitting*, all of the companies involved in some type of pre-release funding scheme make the terms of the purchase/investment almost absurdly clear. Then, some developers go out of their way to say "don't buy this game if..."

Ideas fail. Life happens. Who are the people that break out the pitchforks when 2 peeps trying to make a game in their basement have delayed timelines or release a buggy beta? Why do they feel so wronged when the entire system is set up with risks and rewards clearly laid out? Have they fulfilled every deadline and promise in your personal and professional life? Have you realized every vision or path your ever walked down? I'm not trying to criticize, I just don't get it. Making a video game seems like a hard thing to achieve. If you don't want the risk, wait for a full release, right?

So where does the perception fail? Is there anything distributors or producers could make more clear? I've been so utterly disappointed by one game I actually publicly criticized it. I bought it at full release. It was Beyond Earth, not a bad game. I had just put 2 years (and in some ways more) of anticipation into waiting for its release. I would have payed double what they wanted. I was that excited for a new Alpha Centuri. In retrospect, I wish I hadn't said some very mildly negative things on Twitter. I just wanted them to polish it to the point of any other Civ game.

*My favorite couch, in my living room, while I happen to be wearing pants.
How Is the Perception So Skewed On Early Access, Kick Starter, Etc.

Who are the people that break out the pitchforks when 2 peeps trying to make a game in their basement have delayed timelines or release a buggy beta?

Generally noone actually. People get up in arms when larger companies or well-funded well-vetted studios do it. For example Double Fine with Spacebase DF-9. Double Fine raised plenty of money, plus EA sales, and they know exactly how game development works, they just dumped the work and slapped the 1.0v label on it.

The other problem with all of these systems is that they are labeled and marketed as "Early" "Beta" or similar, that gives the implication that there is a guarantee that the game will be finished. If the dev folds without actually finishing the game, or drops it because it's not what they wanted then people feel they didn't receive what they purchased. The way all of these have been marketed is that you're pre-purchasing a product and as a bonus you get access before official release. If companies want you to invest in a prototype and you get the product as is and you get updates until they're done that's fine but then all of these systems and the way that the companies talk about these systems needs a whole re-branding.

What gets worrisome is when the developers start going in a direction that you as a player no longer find enjoyable. You realize that you aren't the target audience, and you have wasted your time.

Like a game starts out story-driven. But then the developers paste in the next map as a fun and "show what we're doing" area, which doesn't have the story aspects yet, and they decide they want to keep the area without the story. This is could partly be because the other early buyers repeatedly stated that they like the openness of the story-less map, and so it stays that way.
